name: Vera Baker

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for sitting down with me. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, parties or government. Everything you say stays confidential, so you can tell me what you'd say in public and what you really think. Tell me about a normal week at university so far.

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm studying sport and exercise science at a university in a coastal city, in a flat above a bakery with two friends from my church youth group. My week is physiology lectures, a gym practical on Tuesdays, and I coach a girls' netball team on Thursday evenings. I use AI every day to plan training programmes and check my essays. My parents pay for everything, and my dad is a plumber who has his own small firm. I love coaching. The statistics module is the one I put off.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The first picture is called AI Plateau. "Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's good to have a bit of calm. Sport is about people moving, and no one expects an AI to run a netball practice. I'd tell my friends to use AI as a helper and not rely on it for everything.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately I'd feel settled. I already use AI for training plans, so a plateau means I'm ahead of the curve. My degree has a normal path to a decent job as a coach or a trainer. It might not make me rich, but it's steady, and I like steady.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd carry on with the degree and the coaching. I'd keep using AI to plan sessions, and start building a small online business of training plans for local teams. I'd put my coaching money into a savings pot for a gym of my own someday.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. It feels like a fine place to be.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would your own gym look like?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Small, friendly, with a few classes and a bit of equipment. Dad says a trade business can start small and grow, and I think a gym can too. I'd want it in my home town, with families in it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Is that realistic with your degree?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Yes, I think so. Sport science helps with credibility, and being able to use AI for admin and plans keeps my costs low.

feel: **Calm**; it feels like a fine place to be.

Keep coaching the netball team on Thursday evenings

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The second picture is called Steady Disruption. "Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's a big shift, and I'd tell my friends to stay curious and not be afraid of it. I'd say schools and churches should teach young people to use it wisely. I'd also say it's good for people who work hard and bad for those who don't adapt.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately I think my job is safer than most, since coaching and training are about people. But I think office-side sport jobs, like analysts and club admin, shrink. If AI can write plans and track performance, the first rung of a sports career might narrow.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd use AI more, to build a full programme and a simple app for clients. I'd ask a local club for an unpaid internship in performance analysis, so I'd learn how data is used. I'd keep my coaching going, and I'd tell my parents I'm planning ahead.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Energised with a little worry. It feels like an open door that might not stay open.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What do you mean by the door not staying open?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: That the people who start early get the good spots. If I wait until it's obvious, a bigger company will have a sports analytics product and no club will need me. I'd rather build something small now.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you ever feel guilty about replacing a human?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Slightly. I wouldn't want to put a trainer out of work to save a few pounds. But I'd say a tool that helps one coach work with more people is fair.

steps.text: Build a simple client training app with AI help

Keep coaching the netball team through the school year

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The third picture is called AGI by 2028. "Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say two years is too short, and we need leaders who will tell the truth about what's coming. I'd tell my friends to get ready by learning real skills, like coaching and caring for people. I'd also say families and churches have to help those who struggle.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately I'm scared, even though I use AI daily. If AI does thinking work by 2028 and robots do hands-on work by 2031, even coaching could change. I'd be about twenty-one, and I don't know if a degree would be worth much. My dad's plumbing firm feels more solid than my plan.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd ask my parents if I could do a plumbing or electrical apprenticeship alongside my degree. I'd keep building my training app so I have something of my own. I'd save every pound, and I'd pray about it and talk to my pastor before making a big choice.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious. A bit of fear and a bit of faith together.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why plumbing?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Because Dad's work is hands-on and local, and I've watched him fix things my whole life. By 2031 robots may reach it too, but it'll take longer, and people still pay for a person they trust in their house.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would your dad take you on?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: He'd say yes, but he'd also tell me to finish my degree first. He'd say have two things, not one.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fourth picture is called AGI by 2031. "Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years is enough time to build something, if you start now. I'd tell my friends and the church youth group to pick one skill that AI can't copy, like leading a team. I'd also say it's okay to be a bit scared.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately I'd be uneasy, not frightened. I'd graduate in 2029 with a degree and a small business in progress. Then in 2031 AI does most thinking jobs, but I'd already be running a gym and coaching. Robots by 2034 might help with equipment, but people still turn up to be coached by a person.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd finish the degree, run my training app as a small business, and look for a gym space to rent in my home town. I'd keep using AI for admin and bookings, so it's cheap to run. I'd invest any spare money in the gym equipment, bit by bit.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy, but hopeful. I'd rather be building than waiting.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How do you pay for the gym space?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd start with a hall rental, a few classes and a small group. Dad has friends who'd lend tools or help with fitting out. I'd grow it slowly and use my own savings first.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you do if it didn't work?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Go back to coaching in a school or a club, and carry on with the app. A smaller plan is still a plan.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The last picture is called AGI by 2036. "Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is a good length of time, and we should use it to build families, businesses and communities that can stand on their own. I'd tell friends to focus on trust and relationships, because those can't be copied. I'd say ten years makes me hopeful.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately I'd feel calm. By 2036 I'd have a gym with a few staff and a decent client list, and AI would be helping behind the scenes. By 2039, when robots reach physical work, a coach who knows people would still have a place. I might even use robots to carry equipment.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd finish the degree, open a small gym by twenty-five, and add a physio room later. I'd keep AI tools for scheduling and training plans, and I'd hire a young coach. I'd also tithe and save, and start planning a family around then.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm and hopeful. It's the one I'd choose.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you want to teach your own children to work with AI?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Yes, but with rules. I'd want them to know how to think without it first, like learning the road before using the sat-nav. That's how my dad taught me to drive.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would make this ten years go wrong?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: If big gym chains get cheap robot trainers and push everyone out. Then I'd need a niche, like faith-based fitness groups or classes for older people, where a human and a community matter.

Focus on **trust and relationships**, which can't be copied.

A coach who **knows people** would still have a place in 2039.

Hire a young **coach** and use AI for scheduling.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028 worries me most, because it leaves no time to build anything of your own. What would help is practical training, family and church support, and small business help for people like my dad.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Just that people can adapt and still keep their values. I use AI every day and I still go to church, coach a team, and call my grandma. I'd like the future to have room for all of that.

portrait: Vera studies **sport and exercise science** and uses AI every day for plans and essays.
She is traditional and faith-minded, but adaptive and quick to **build things**.
Her dad's plumbing firm shapes her plan: start small, grow, and have a **trade-like** back-up.
She is calm when time allows and anxious in the **two-year** picture.
Her main dream is her own gym, run with AI but powered by trust.
biggestWorry: AGI by 2028 worries her most, because it leaves **no time** to build anything of her own.
whatWouldHelp: Practical training, **family and church support**, and help for small businesses.
